bennett_cardinality_statement_review.status: mathematical statement audit; not a machine-checked proof
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.reference: M. A. Bennett, J. reine angew. Math. 535 (2001), 1-49, Theorem 1.1
assumptions: S is a finite set of primes containing 2 and 3
n>=3 and H,T,r are positive integers
H divides n-2 and 6 H r^3 = T n(n-1)(n-2)
v_p(T) is divisible by 3 for every prime p outside S
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.reduction: If p outside S divides n or n-1, it divides neither 6H nor the other two consecutive factors. Valuations imply 3 divides v_p(n) or v_p(n-1), respectively. Thus their unique positive cube-free cores A,B are supported on S and coprime.
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.cardinality_reason: Each prime has five placements: absent, exponent 1 or 2 in A, or exponent 1 or 2 in B. Swapping A,B has only the fixed pair (1,1), which has no solution in positive cubic bases. Bennett's theorem applied to |A x^3-B y^3|=1 gives at most one positive base pair per remaining unordered core pair; n is the larger of the two terms.
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.distinct_first_index_bound: (5^|S|-1)/2, uniformly in H and all allowed exponents of T
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.full_auxiliary_tuple_finiteness: Also impose 3n<r<10n/3. For each n there are floor((n-1)/3) integer choices of r, finitely many positive H dividing n-2, and at most one T for each n,H,r. If gcd(H,T)=1, n,r uniquely determine H=A0/g and T=r^3/g, where A0=binomial(n,3), g=gcd(A0,r^3). Without a bound on r, the first-index bound alone does not give finiteness of all auxiliary tuples.
bennett_cardinality_statement_review.scope_limit: This does not classify the original four-variable equation.

reports.coverage_method: all 3^s cube-free cores squared, then gcd(A,B)=1
